clue.text: Second round indicating the end for some bars

definitions.text: indicating the end for some bars
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for the noun: the stressed back beats fall late in each bar

blocks.note: to second a proposal is to back it
a police officer's round is a beat

explanation.surface: A second round of drinks signals that the pubs are about to close.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bars' looks like pubs at closing time, but they are musical bars; the second and fourth beats of a bar carry the emphasis.
explanation.definitionFit: A backbeat is the accent on the later beats of each musical bar, typical of rock and pop rhythm.

clue.text: English artist's holding blazer?

indicators.note: something holding another keeps it inside, so the painter's name wraps round the letter

explanation.surface: An English painter is wearing a blazer, the jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blazer' looks like a jacket; the question mark warns it means something that blazes.
explanation.definitionFit: A beacon is a signal fire lit on a hill, so it is literally something that blazes.

clue.text: Make official pet's name up, in case of candidacy

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the name from bottom to top
in places the name inside the outer letters of the following word
the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

blocks.note: first and last letters of candidacy
Fido is the stock name for a pet dog

explanation.surface: A candidate's paperwork formally records the name of their pet.
explanation.definitionFit: To codify rules is to set them down formally as an official code.

clue.text: Donkey's brief retreat

indicators.note: making a word brief cuts it short, dropping its final letter

blocks.note: a burrow is an animal's retreat

explanation.surface: A donkey takes a quick break somewhere sheltered.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is': the donkey is the shortened retreat.
explanation.definitionFit: A burro is a small donkey, the Spanish word used in the American southwest.

clue.text: Clamour follows after dressing daughter in rubber in panto

blocks.note: à la means in the manner of, after
a din is a loud noise

explanation.surface: A noisy scene breaks out after a daughter is dressed in a rubber costume for the pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber' looks like the material of a costume, but it is someone who rubs; the clamour comes last as it follows the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: In the pantomime story the hero summons the genie by rubbing a magic lamp, so he is the famous rubber.

clue.text: Sailor misspelled sail, perhaps, and let himself down?

indicators.note: a misspelling changes one letter of a word, swapping a vowel for another

blocks.note: the word sail with its A turned into an E

explanation.surface: A sailor made a spelling mistake and disappointed himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let himself down' reads as disappointment but is literal: descending a rope. The German Seil, rope, is where the word comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: To abseil is to lower yourself down a cliff or wall on a rope.

clue.text: Lovely tailored fit, blue with gold lining

indicators.note: tailored clothing is cut and reshaped, so the letters are refashioned
a lining sits inside a garment, so the metal goes in among the other letters

explanation.surface: A well-fitted blue suit with a gold lining looks lovely.
explanation.definitionFit: Lovely and beautiful are synonyms for attractive.

clue.text: Record company acquiring modern top 100 firm

indicators.note: acquiring something takes it in, so the record label holds the slang word

blocks.note: phat is modern slang for excellent, tip-top

explanation.surface: A record label buys up one of the hundred biggest modern companies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firm' sits beside 'company' as if it meant a business, but it is an adjective meaning forceful.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm statement is forceful and decisive, which is what emphatic means.

clue.text: Lord's opener not starting game with main opener

indicators.note: the opener of a word is its first letter
not starting means the first letter is left off

blocks.note: key means main, as in a key point

explanation.surface: At Lord's, an opening batsman misses the start of the match.
explanation.walkthrough: Lord's is the London cricket ground, so 'opener' looks like an opening batsman; the last word is the definition, a thing that opens a door.
explanation.definitionFit: A latchkey is the key to an outer door's latch, so it is an opener.

clue.text: Governor replaced half of Mars lander

indicators.note: something replaced is put back differently, so the letters are rearranged
half of a word keeps only its first two of four letters

explanation.surface: Mission control replaced part of a spacecraft that landed on Mars.
explanation.definitionFit: An alderman is a senior member of a town or borough council, one who governs it.

clue.text: Alternative to rap etc?

indicators.note: an alternative version of these letters is a different arrangement of them

explanation.surface: Someone asks what music could replace rap and the like.
explanation.walkthrough: Rap seems to be the music, but it is a rebuke; the whole clue is both the wordplay and a synonym hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: To carpet someone is British slang for to reprimand them, an alternative word for a rap over the knuckles.

clue.text: Band leaders – or bandleaders? – only partially recalled

indicators.note: only part of these words is used, the answer sitting inside them
recalled means called back, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: the letters straddling the end of leaders, or, and the start of bandleaders

explanation.surface: Someone half-remembers whether it was band leaders or bandleaders.
explanation.definitionFit: Bros were a British boy band of the late 1980s, led by twins Matt and Luke Goss.

clue.text: Defender, perhaps Pole, tackling American in advance

indicators.note: tackling something means getting to grips with it, wrapping round it
in places the combined piece inside the next word

blocks.note: to advance a suggestion is to offer it

explanation.surface: A Polish defender tackles an American player before the ball arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The Defender is the Land Rover model, not a footballer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Land Rover Defender is a rugged vehicle built for driving off the road, an example of the class.

clue.text: Favourite to lose games with a head coach

indicators.note: to lose letters is to drop them from the word

blocks.note: a pet is a favourite, as in a pet project
as in five pounds a head

explanation.surface: The favourite is set to lose its games when it has a new head coach.
explanation.definitionFit: To coach someone is to train or teach them.

clue.text: Spare article ultimately not needed

indicators.note: the last letter is not needed, so the word loses its end

blocks.note: an article is an item, a thing

explanation.surface: A spare item turns out not to be needed in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a grammatical a, an or the, but it is an object.
explanation.definitionFit: Spare can mean lean or scanty, as in a spare frame, which is thin.

clue.text: Fine bit of bread with unknown fish

blocks.note: a hunk is a thick piece of bread
algebra's unknowns are x, y and z

explanation.surface: A meal: a chunk of bread served with some mystery fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Hunky-dory is informal for fine, everything all right.

clue.text: Do ask to hold service without clothing

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it within, so the verb wraps round the next piece
without its clothing the word is stripped of its outer letters

blocks.note: to sue for peace is to ask for it
an office is a church service

explanation.surface: Someone requests a church service without the formal clothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' leads the clue as if an instruction, but it is the definition, as in 'that will do'.
explanation.definitionFit: When something will do, it is enough, and to suffice is to be enough.

clue.text: Liberal wearing former Truss costume

indicators.note: whoever is wearing something has it on the outside, so the letter goes inside

blocks.note: back as in back then, formerly
to truss is to tie up

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician dresses up as the former prime minister Liz Truss.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz Truss was briefly UK prime minister, which is what 'former Truss' suggests; here truss is just the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Black tie is the dress code for a dinner jacket and bow tie, a formal outfit.

clue.text: Turned on after joke about content of salt and pepper

indicators.note: the content of a word is what lies inside, its inner letters
about means around, so the prank goes round the inner letters
a word turned round is read backwards

explanation.surface: Someone is turned on after a joke about what is in the salt and pepper pots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt and pepper' reads as one condiment pair, but only salt is wordplay; pepper is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A jalapeño is a hot green chilli, a kind of pepper.

clue.text: The French are claiming Northern Rhodesia's capital, I'm discovering

definitions.note: a self-description: the learner is the 'I' doing the discovering

indicators.note: claiming something takes it into your possession, so the verb wraps round a letter
a word's capital is its capital letter, the first one

explanation.surface: I am finding out that the French are laying claim to the capital of Northern Rhodesia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Northern Rhodesia's capital' looks like a geography question (Lusaka), but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A learner is a person still finding things out, a student who is discovering.

clue.text: European abandoning final of ping pong

indicators.note: abandoning something leaves it behind, so a letter is dropped
the final of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A European player walks out of the final of a ping pong tournament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ping pong' reads as table tennis; split, pong is the definition, British slang for a bad smell.
explanation.definitionFit: A pong is a stink, and reek is a strong unpleasant smell.

clue.text: Marvel's first class exploit

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Marvel's top-class superhero exploit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploit' reads as a heroic deed, a noun, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To milk a situation is to exploit it for all it is worth.

clue.text: Measure of speed in electronic engine

blocks.note: Mach number, speed relative to sound

explanation.surface: A technical measure of how fast an electronic engine runs.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine is a machine that converts energy into motion, so the two are near synonyms.

clue.text: Starmer leading popular race

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer is ahead in a popularity contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Race' sounds political, but it is a track-cycling event.
explanation.definitionFit: Keirin is a track cycling event in which riders follow a pacer before sprinting, an Olympic race.

clue.text: Nervous individual departs, say, northwards

indicators.note: in a down entry, going northwards means reading upwards, backwards

explanation.surface: A nervous person sets off heading north.
explanation.definitionFit: To be on edge is an idiom for being tense and jumpy.

clue.text: Cautious about dangerous missing setter

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so a letter is taken out

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as I

explanation.surface: Wary of something hazardous now that the setter has gone missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Chary means wary, reluctant to take risks.

clue.text: Cryptic clue concept needing name of a mathematician

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling and disguised, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Coming up with a cryptic clue idea requires a mathematician's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Euclidean refers to Euclid, the Greek geometer, as in Euclidean geometry.

clue.text: Recipe initially welcomed by a fan of basic course?

indicators.note: initially means at the start, taking the first letter
being welcomed by someone means being taken in, placed inside

blocks.note: to be into something is to be a fan of it

explanation.surface: A beginner cook welcomes a recipe for a simple course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' tempts as part of a meal beside the recipe; it is a course of study.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is an introductory course covering the basics of a subject.

clue.text: Tic tac rival originally getting capital backing

indicators.note: originally means at the origin, the first letters of these words
backing means going backwards, so the city is read in reverse

blocks.note: first letters of tac and rival

explanation.surface: A rival mint brand to Tic Tac gets financial backing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tic Tac is a mint brand; splitting it, tic is the definition and tac only gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tic is an involuntary twitch, a kind of tremor or shake.

clue.text: Spent months with journalist shadowing Italian club

explanation.surface: A journalist spent months following an Italian football club.
explanation.walkthrough: The journalist shadows, that is follows, the club, so editor comes last.
explanation.definitionFit: To winter somewhere is to spend the cold season there, a few months.

clue.text: I'm surprised by refusal to return Caesar salad, say

definitions.note: strictly the dish is eponymous; the eponym is the name it carries

indicators.note: to return is to go back, so the combined letters are read backwards

blocks.note: my! is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A diner is surprised when the kitchen refuses to send back a Caesar salad.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar salad is named after its creator, the restaurateur Caesar Cardini, not Julius Caesar.
explanation.definitionFit: An eponym is a name taken from a person, as Caesar salad takes its name from Caesar Cardini.

clue.text: Snug cat in pan

blocks.note: a snug is a cosy room, a den
the ounce is the snow leopard

explanation.surface: A cat curled up cosily inside a pan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pan' looks like a cooking pot; it is the verb meaning to criticise harshly.
explanation.definitionFit: To pan a show is to slate it, and to denounce is to condemn publicly.
